title: ABO Blood Group System: Forward/Reverse Typing and ABO Discrepancies
summary: The ABO system is the most important blood group in transfusion medicine. This lesson covers the biochemistry of A and B antigens, how forward (cell) and reverse (serum) typing are performed and interpreted, and how to recognize and resolve ABO discrepancies before blood is issued.
objectives: Explain the biochemical basis of A and B antigens on red cells and the genetic basis of ABO transferases.
Perform and interpret forward and reverse ABO typing, including expected reactions for each ABO group.
Classify ABO discrepancies by phase and describe a practical approach to resolving them before transfusion.
Explain why reverse typing is unreliable in newborns and in certain immunocompromised patients.

highYield: Group A red cells carry A antigen; plasma contains anti-B. Group B red cells carry B antigen; plasma contains anti-A.
Group O red cells carry neither A nor B antigen; plasma contains anti-A and anti-B. Group AB carries both antigens and neither antibody.
Forward and reverse typing must agree; any discrepancy must be resolved before issuing blood components.
Reverse typing is weak or absent in newborns because naturally occurring isohemagglutinins develop over the first months of life.
A and B antigens are carbohydrate structures; the O allele produces a nonfunctional transferase, so no A or B antigen is made.
quickReview.mnemonic: O has nO antigens and bOth antibodies; AB has Both antigens and No antibodies.

deepStudy.introduction: ABO compatibility is the single most critical safety check in transfusion therapy. An ABO-incompatible red cell transfusion causes acute intravascular hemolysis and can be fatal, so the laboratory must establish a patient's ABO group with certainty. Two independent tests provide that certainty: forward (cell) grouping, which detects A and B antigens on the patient's red cells, and reverse (serum) grouping, which detects expected isohemagglutinins in the patient's plasma. When the two tests agree, the ABO group is confirmed. When they disagree, the laboratory has an ABO discrepancy, and no ABO-identical blood should be issued until the discrepancy is explained. This lesson builds the antigen biochemistry first, then walks through both typing phases, and finishes with a systematic approach to discrepancies.

sections.heading: Molecular basis of A and B antigens
sections.body: A and B antigens are not proteins encoded directly by the ABO gene; they are carbohydrate epitopes carried on glycoproteins and glycolipids on the red cell membrane and in secretions. The ABO gene on chromosome 9 encodes a glycosyltransferase that transfers a specific sugar from a nucleotide donor onto an H substance precursor: the A transferase adds N-acetylgalactosamine to create the A antigen, while the B transferase adds galactose to create the B antigen. The common O allele carries a single-base deletion that produces a truncated, nonfunctional enzyme, so the H substance remains unmodified and no A or B antigen is expressed. Because A and B transferases compete for the same H substrate, group AB individuals express both antigens on each cell, whereas group O individuals express neither. The antigens are well developed at birth, which is why forward typing is reliable in newborns. By contrast, the corresponding antibodies, anti-A and anti-B, are not genetically encoded; they are naturally occurring isohemagglutinins, largely IgM, produced in response to environmental antigens resembling A and B structures on gut bacteria and plants. This Landsteiner rule, that individuals make antibodies against the A or B antigens they lack, is the foundation of reverse typing.

sections.heading: Forward (cell) typing
sections.body: Forward typing tests the patient's red cells with known, potent antisera: anti-A, anti-B, and often anti-A,B (a blend useful for detecting weak A subgroups) or anti-D for Rh typing. The procedure is simple: patient red cells are washed or suspended in saline, mixed with typing reagent, centrifuged, and read for agglutination. Agglutination or hemolysis with anti-A indicates the presence of A antigen; agglutination with anti-B indicates B antigen; agglutination with both indicates group AB; agglutination with neither indicates group O. Forward typing is antigen based and is dependable at any age because A and B antigens are fully expressed at birth. Common technical problems include using a cell suspension that is too dense or too weak, failing to read reactions at the proper phase, and misinterpreting mixed-field agglutination, which may indicate a recent transfusion, chimerism, or a bone marrow transplant rather than a simple subgroup. Automated and solid-phase platforms perform the same logic, but every instrument result still requires verification according to local policy.

sections.heading: Reverse (serum) typing and its limitations
sections.body: Reverse typing tests the patient's plasma or serum against known reagent red cells: A1 cells and B cells, and sometimes A2 cells. The expected pattern mirrors the forward result: group A plasma agglutinates B cells only; group B plasma agglutinates A1 cells only; group O plasma agglutinates both; group AB plasma agglutinates neither. Reverse typing is performed at room temperature and read after immediate spin, because isohemagglutinins are predominantly IgM and react optimally at lower temperatures. The strength of reverse reactions is graded, and weak or missing reactions have several explanations. Newborns lack isohemagglutinins because maternal IgG anti-A and anti-B do not reliably cause reverse reactions and the infant's own production matures over roughly the first three to six months of life; reverse typing is therefore unreliable in infants under about four months. The elderly, patients with hypogammaglobulinemia, and heavily immunosuppressed patients may also have weak or absent isohemagglutinins. Conversely, reverse reactions may be falsely strong or diffuse because of high-titer cold autoantibodies, rouleaux formation in hypergammaglobulinemia, or unexpected alloantibodies such as anti-A1 in some A2 individuals. Any disagreement between phases is an ABO discrepancy and demands resolution.

sections.heading: ABO discrepancies: causes and resolution
sections.body: ABO discrepancies are grouped by where the problem appears. Group 1 discrepancies involve the forward typing: expected antigen reactions are weaker than expected or missing. Classic causes include subgroups of A, most often A2 or weaker variants such as Ax, which may type as O with anti-A but show weak reactions with anti-A,B; acquired B, in which bacterial enzymes modify the A antigen so that group A cells react with anti-B reagent (classically reported in patients with gram-negative sepsis or colorectal disease, whose serum still contains anti-B that does not react with their own altered cells at the proper conditions); and mixed-field reactions from recent transfusion. Group 2 discrepancies involve the reverse typing: unexpected or missing antibody reactions. Causes include missing isohemagglutinins in newborns or immunosuppressed patients, anti-A1 in A2 patients, cold autoantibodies causing panagglutination, rouleaux, and passively acquired antibodies from plasma-containing products or IVIG. A practical resolution algorithm is: repeat testing in duplicate from a freshly collected specimen to rule out clerical error or contamination; inspect the cell suspension and reagents; test the cells with anti-A,B and lectins such as Dolichos biflorus, which agglutinates A1 but not A2 cells; incubate reverse typing at 4 degrees Celsius to enhance weak cold antibodies; use a saline replacement technique to dissolve rouleaux; perform an autocontrol; review the patient's transfusion and transplant history; and, when necessary, refer to a reference laboratory for adsorption-elution, saliva studies for secretor status, or molecular ABO genotyping. No unit should be issued until forward and reverse results agree and the patient's group is confirmed.

deepStudy.clinicalSignificance: ABO-incompatible transfusion is a preventable, frequently fatal event caused by clerical errors and unresolved discrepancies. Confirming ABO group with two independent phases, labeling specimens at the bedside, and refusing to issue blood in the face of an unexplained discrepancy are the core safety behaviors of immunohematology. ABO group also matters beyond red cells: plasma and platelet components carry donor isohemagglutinins, so ABO-compatible or group-specific plasma is preferred, and high-titer anti-A or anti-B in group O plasma can cause hemolysis when given to non-O recipients.
deepStudy.labInterpretation: Interpret forward and reverse results as a pair, never in isolation. A full concordant pattern (for example, forward A, reverse anti-B) confirms the group. Weak forward reactions suggest A subgroups or mixed fields; strong unexpected reverse reactions suggest cold antibodies or rouleaux; missing reverse reactions suggest age or immune status. When reporting, document the discrepancy, the resolution steps, and the final interpretation. Reference intervals for isohemagglutinin titers vary by laboratory, method, and population, and are not used for routine patient typing; always verify interpretation against your local blood bank standard operating procedure.

examTraps: Reverse typing in newborns is weak or absent because naturally occurring isohemagglutinins are not yet produced; do not expect concordant reverse typing in an infant under roughly four months of age.
Group O does not mean 'no antibodies': group O plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B, which is why group O is the universal red cell donor but not the universal plasma donor.
Acquired B makes group A cells appear to be AB in forward typing, but the patient's serum contains anti-B; the discrepancy resolves with knowledge of the clinical context and proper test conditions.
